title.en: Okonorote and the Pit into the Lower World (Warrau Version)
title.zh: 奧科諾羅特與通下界之穴（瓦勞版）

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河瓦勞之地

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Warraus begin their story not with the manufacture of bodies but from a time when their ancestors lived in sky-land. There Okonorote, a famous hunter, followed a bird for many days; his arrow pierced it at last, but the game fell down into a deep pit — and looking down Okonorote saw daylight below, and discerned a land on which many kinds of four-footed animals were walking. With the help of his tribe he hung a long bush-rope down toward the earth and climbed down it. The Warraus who had remained in sky-land so appreciated the venison he brought home that they determined to move to the land below; after many had descended, a woman stuck in the hole and could never be moved — so those already on earth had to remain there, and those still in sky-land remained there. The True Caribs tell the story with one difference: their object in coming down was to clean the earth, which was evidently very dirty.
summary.zh: 瓦勞人言其祖居天上。獵人奧科諾羅特逐鳥多日，末射中之；鳥墮深穴。俯視見穴下有天光，更有大地，走獸成群。族人助之垂長藤而下。歸而携鹿肉；天上部族嘗之，皆願遷居下界。既降多人，一婦卡於穴口，推挽不動——已降者遂留人間，未降者留天上。真加勒比人則謂其下地之目的乃掃除大地之穢。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Variant of the existing Warau sky-descent record.

passages.text: The Warraus, without troubling their minds as to the first manufacture of the bodily shapes which we see, begin their story from a time when their ancestors lived in sky-land. Up there one of their number, named Okonorote, was a famous hunter. On one occasion he followed a bird for many days without finding opportunity to shoot it. At length he succeeded, his arrow piercing the bird. But the game fell down into a deep pit, and was apparently lost.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Okonorote, looking down into the pit, saw daylight below, and before long was able to discern down below a land on which many kinds of four-footed animals were walking. With the help of his tribe he hung a long piece of bush-rope down toward the earth, and then climbed down this. After much successful hunting he climbed home again, taking with him some venison. The Warraus who had remained in sky-land, never having tasted such food before, appreciated it so highly that they determined to move to the land below.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: After many had descended, a woman — who according to some was with child, according to others was very fat — stuck in the hole in sky-land, and though the other members of the tribe pushed and pulled from above and below, it was never possible to move her. So the Warraus who were already on earth had to remain there, and those who were still in sky-land remained there. The True Caribs have a story which differs from this of the Warraus only in that the former represent that their object in coming down from sky-land to earth was to clean the latter place, which was evidently very dirty.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

title.en: Korobona and the Stump of the Pond

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍沼地瓦勞之地

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Warraus tell how the first Carib was born, and how the enmity between the two tribes began. There was a pond in which the Warraus feared to bathe; two women ventured into the water, and Korobona, touching the stump of a tree which rose over the surface, was seized by it and made his wife. Her brothers, jealous of their sister's honor, wished to kill her child; it soon died. A second child, a boy, she hid in the forest; the brothers shot their arrows into him and left him as dead, but the mother nursed and reared him. When he was a big boy they attacked him and cut his body in small pieces — and from the grave in which the mother buried him rose an Indian more powerful and more fierce than any Warrau had ever been. He was the first Carib, who, with his descendants, waged perpetual war on the Warraus and reduced them to their present miserable state.
summary.zh: 瓦勞人言首加勒比之生與二族之仇。池中有樹樁，人皆畏不敢浴；科羅波納觸之，樁攫之為妻。兄惡其辱，欲殺其嬰；嬰旋死。再生一男，匿於林中；兄射之而去，母育之得活。及長，兄攻而碎其體——母葬之，墓中起一勇士，猛逾瓦勞之任何男子。是為首加勒比；其子孫與瓦勞永戰，遂使瓦勞淪於今日之慘境。

sensitivity.note: Warrau oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Variant cross-ref to Roth's origin-of-Caribs records.

passages.text: Once upon a time there was a pond in which, as is often the case, the Warraus feared to bathe. At last two Indian women ventured into the water. Presently one of the women, named Korobona, touched the stump of a tree which rose over the surface of the water, and immediately the stump seized her and made her his wife. Then Korobona returned home, where after some time a child was born. The brothers, jealous of their sister's honour, wished to kill it, but eventually consented to spare it. The child, however, soon died.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Korobona went back to the pond, and again saw the stump. Once more a child was born, this time a boy. The mother, remembering her brothers' threats on the previous occasion, hid the child in the forest. But the brothers discovered their sister's secret, and, having shot their arrows into the boy, left him as dead. But the mother nursed her child, revived it, and succeeded in rearing it. It was not till the child was a big boy that the brothers discovered that he still lived. Then they attacked him, and cut his body in small pieces.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: From the grave in which the mother buried the victim rose an Indian more powerful and more fierce than any Warrau had ever been. He was the first Carib, who, with his descendants, waged perpetual war on the Warraus and reduced them to their present miserable state.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Food-Tree and the Watchers (Carib Version)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Caribs say that when they first arrived on earth from sky-land, cassava, plantains, and all useful vegetables grew on one huge tree. This tree was first discovered by a tapir, who grew fat on the fruits which fell from its branches. The Caribs, finding the new land a poor place without food, set the woodpecker to watch him — but the woodpecker, flying after the tapir, could not resist the temptation to tap the trees for insects, and the tapir, hearing the noise, knew he was followed and went another way. Then the Caribs sent a rat, who traced the tapir to his food-tree but, having agreed with the tapir to share the food quietly, persuaded the Caribs that he too had failed — until they found him asleep one day with corn still in his mouth, woke him and compelled him to show the tree. Each man took pieces of the felled tree and planted them in a field of his own; so from that day each Indian has had his own cassava-field.
summary.zh: 加勒比人言初至大地時，木薯、香蕉與百蔬皆生於一巨樹。貘先得之，食落果而肥。加勒比人饑而蹤之；啄木鳥窺之，忍不住叩木覓蟲，貘聞聲而遁。再遣田鼠；鼠與貘私約分食，詭言無所獲——後眾見其口含穀而睡，喚醒逼其指樹。伐而分之，各植於己田；自是印第安人各有薯田。

sensitivity.note: Carib oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Variant of Roth's Allepdntepo record.

passages.text: The Caribs say that when they first arrived on earth from sky-land, cassava, plantains, and all useful vegetables grew on one huge tree. This tree was first discovered by a tapir, who grew fat on the fruits which fell from its branches. The Caribs, who as yet had found the new land a poor place and without food, were eager to find where the tapir fed. So they set the woodpecker to watch him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: But the woodpecker as he flew through the forest after the tapir could not resist the temptation to tap the trees for insects, and the tapir, hearing the noise, knew he was followed, and went another way. Then the Caribs sent a rat, who stealthily succeeded in tracing the tapir to his food-tree; but the rat, having agreed with the tapir quietly to share the food, persuaded the Caribs that he too had failed in the quest. But the Caribs, finding the rat asleep one day with corn still in his mouth, woke him and compelled him to show the tree.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Caribs took their stone axes, and after many months' hard work succeeded in felling it. Each man took pieces of the tree and planted them in a field of his own; so from that day each Indian has had his own cassava-field.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Flood from the Basket: the Howler's Throat and the Trumpeter's Legs
title.zh: 籃下洪水：吼猴之喉與鶴之脛

region.zh: 蓋亞那馬扎魯尼上游阿卡瓦之地

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Ackawoi tell that the acourie was the original discoverer of the food-tree, and that one single man — their traditional ancestor — assisted by various animals cut it down. From the stump of the felled tree a flood began to flow out onto the land, but before much harm was done its flow was stopped by one man, who inverted an empty basket over the spring of water. For some time the water was confined under the basket; but at last the brown monkey, suspecting that something very good must be hidden under the carefully tended basket, cautiously raised it and peeped under. In an instant the flood rushed out, carrying away the monkey and overflowing the whole land. Then the man, with all manner of animals, took refuge up in a tall kokerite palm. Most of the fugitives remained patiently during the flood, but the red howling-monkey began to roar so loudly that his throat swelled and has remained extended ever since — that is the reason of the curious bony drum in the throat of this animal. The trumpet-bird flew down in such a hurry that he alighted in an ants' nest, and the hungry insects fastened on his legs, which had before been fairly thick, and gnawed them down to their present spindle-like size.
summary.zh: 阿卡瓦人言食樹乃刺鼠先得，其祖一人力伐之。樹樁湧泉成洪；一人倒置空籃於泉上而塞之。棕猴疑籃下藏美物，潛掀而窺之——洪即暴發，沖猴而去，盡沒大地。人與眾獸避於高柯基里棕。紅吼猴怒吼，喉腫而至今長存——故其喉中有骨鼓；鶴鳥急降蟻塚，脛為蟻齧細如今。

sensitivity.note: Akawai oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Flood-cluster record.

passages.text: The Ackawoi tell a tale which differs from the Carib story of the food-tree only in that they say that the acourie was the original discoverer of the food-tree, and that one single man, apparently their traditional ancestor, assisted by various animals, cut it down. From the stump of the felled tree a flood began to flow out on to the land, but before much harm was done the flow of water was stopped by one man, who inverted an empty basket over the spring of water and so stopped its flow.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: For some time the water was confined under the basket. But at last the brown monkey, curious, and suspecting that something very good must be hidden under the carefully tended basket, cautiously raised it and peeped under. In an instant the flood rushed out, carrying away the monkey, and overflowing the whole land. Then the man, with all manner of animals, took refuge up in a tall kokerite palm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Most of the fugitives remained patiently during the flood, but the red howling-monkey, getting excited, began to roar, and roared so loudly that his throat swelled, and has remained extended ever since — that is the reason of the curious bony drum in the throat of this animal. Meanwhile the trumpet-bird flew down in such a hurry that he alighted in an ants' nest, and the hungry insects fastened on his legs, which had before been fairly thick, and gnawed them down to their present spindle-like size.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Alligator Lost His Tongue

region.zh: 蓋亞那馬扎魯尼上游阿卡瓦之地

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: When the flood had subsided, the man began to rub two pieces of wood to make fire, and the first spark generated in this way is very small. The bush-turkey, at a moment when the man was looking away, swallowed this spark, mistaking it for a fire-fly, and then flew quickly away: the spark burned the bush-turkey's throat, and that is the reason why to this day those birds have a red wattle on their throats. Meanwhile the man, missing his spark, saw the alligator, who was then a gentle brute but ugly, standing near. Immediately the other animals, agreeing in their abhorrence of the ugliness of the alligator, raised a shout that it was he who had taken the spark. Whereupon the man, angry and impatient, tore out the tongue of the supposed culprit. And this is the reason why alligators have ever since had such very rudimentary tongues, and also why they wage perpetual war on other beasts.
summary.zh: 洪水既退，人始鑽木取火；初出之火星甚微。火雞誤為螢而吞之，喉灼成赤垂——至今猶然。人失火而見鱷——古性溫而貌醜——立於近旁。眾獸憎其醜，齊呼曰：『火乃鱷竊也！』人怒，拔其舌。故鱷之舌今甚短，且與百獸永戰不休。

sensitivity.note: Akawai oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Fire-theft cluster record.

passages.text: The others having descended more cautiously and safely, the man began to rub two pieces of wood to make fire. Now the first spark generated in this way is very small. The bush-turkey, at a moment when the man was looking away, swallowed this spark, mistaking it for a fire-fly, and then flew quickly away. The spark burned the bush-turkey's throat, and that is the reason why to this day those birds have a red wattle on their throats.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Meanwhile, the man missing his spark, saw the alligator, who was then a gentle brute, but ugly, standing near. Immediately the other animals, agreeing in their abhorrence of the ugliness of the alligator, raised a shout that it was he who had taken the spark. Whereupon the man, angry and impatient, tore out the tongue of the supposed culprit. And this is the reason why alligators have ever since had such very rudimentary tongues, and also why they wage perpetual war on other beasts. That is all that is known of the story.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun's Fish-Dam and the Alligator's Scales

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地（據布雷特）

texts.period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; retold 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Sun one day came down to fish. Like any other Indian, he built a dam across the mouth of a fish-haunted stream to retain the prey; but in his absence the otters broke his dam, and the fish escaped. Then the Sun rebuilt it and placed a woodpecker to watch it. One day the woodpecker tapped very loudly, and the Sun came to see what was the matter: this time it was the alligator who was trying to do damage. So the Sun drove him away by striking him again and again with a huge club — thus were made those marks which we think are scales, to be seen on the alligator to this day.
summary.zh: 一日日神下凡捕魚；如常人然，於多魚溪口築壩蓄之。日神不在，水獺毀壩，魚皆遁。日神重築，以啄木鳥守之。一日鳥叩甚急；日神至視之，乃鱷欲害也。遂以巨杖連擊而逐之——鱷身上所謂鱗者，即杖痕也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett, retold by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, the woodpecker tapping very loudly, the sun came to see what was the matter. This time it was the alligator who was trying to do damage. So the Sun drove him away by striking him again and again with a huge club. Thus were made those marks which we think are scales, which are to be seen on the alligator to this day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

texts.period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; retold 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: A young Arawak chose as his wife a king-vulture; an Indian, when he marries, goes to live with his wife's father, so he went to sky-land and was well received by the vulture's people. But when after a time he announced his intention of paying a visit to his own people, the vultures were enraged, and set him on top of a tall awarra-palm whose trunk is covered with terrible thorns. There he remained until some spiders, feeling pity, spun a cord by which he descended. For many years he tried to get back to his wife, but the vultures would have nothing more to say to him; at last the other birds, taking compassion, carried him to sky-land and helped him to fight the vultures, whose settlement was burned over their heads. In the plundering the trumpet-bird and heron rolled each other in the ashes — the grey back and the all-grey — the owl opened a carefully-done-up package and out came the darkness; and the Arawak on whose behalf the war was waged fought with and was killed by his own son by his vulture wife.
summary.zh: 一阿拉瓦克少年娶王鷲為妻；依俗往岳家——即天界——鷲族善待之。後告歸省，鷲族怒，置之高阿瓦拉棕之巔，幹生惡刺。蛛憐之，結繩而下。經年求復，鷲不納；群鳥憫之，載之上天，助其伐鷲，焚其居。分贓之際，鶴與鷺滾於灰——一得灰背一得通灰；鴞啟密裹之包，黑闇出焉。而為之興師之阿拉瓦克，竟為其鷲妻所生之子所殺。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett, retold by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically. Variant of birds-markings-war record.

passages.text: A similar tale tells how a young Arawak chose as his wife a king-vulture. Now an Indian man, when he marries, goes to live with his wife's father. So the Arawak went to sky-land and was well received by the vulture's people. But when after a time he announced his intention of paying a visit to his own people, the vultures were enraged, and set him on top of a tall awarra-palm, the trunk of which is covered with terrible thorns. There he remained until some spiders, feeling pity, spun a cord by which he descended.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then for many years he tried to get back to his wife, but the vultures would have nothing more to say to him. But at last the other birds, taking compassion on him, carried him to sky-land and helped him to fight the vultures. The latter having been driven into their own houses, their whole settlement was burned over their heads. The Arawak on whose behalf this war was waged fought with, and was killed by, his own son by his vulture wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the other birds began to quarrel over the plunder. The trumpet-bird and the heron got so angry that they fought and rolled each other in the ashes, which is the reason why the former bird has ever since had a grey back, and why the latter has been grey all over. Taking advantage of the confusion, the owl, prowling about, found a package so carefully done up that he thought it must contain something very valuable. So he opened it, and out came the darkness in which he has ever since had to live.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Man Adrift over Kaieteur Fall

region.zh: 蓋亞那波塔羅河凱厄圖爾瀑

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: At the Kaieteur fall there is, in mid-stream a few hundred yards below the fall, a long narrow island shaped much like one of the wood-skins, the bark-boats used by the Ackawoi of that river; and at the side of the river close to the foot of the column of water is a curiously regular rectangular rock shaped like the pegall, the basket in which the Indian packs his properties. Once upon a time, say the Ackawoi, there was on the savannah above the fall an Indian settlement in which lived an old man so worn out and useless from age that in his feet the jiggers buried themselves unmolested — a scandal and a nuisance to his fellows. So they put the old man with his pegall into a woodskin, launched it on the river, and allowed it to drift over the fall. The old man was never seen again; but his woodskin became the island in the river below the fall, and his pegall turned to stone, and remains to this day.
summary.zh: 凱厄圖爾瀑下數百步，河中有狹長之島，形如阿卡瓦人之皮舟；瀑腳旁有方正之石，狀若印第安人裝物之皮籃。阿卡瓦人言：瀑上草原舊有村落，中有老翁，衰廢無用，足中沙蚤叢生，為眾所憎。眾遂置翁及其籃於皮舟，順流而下，任其墮瀑。翁遂不復見；其舟化為瀑下之島，其籃化石，至今猶存。

sensitivity.note: Ackawai tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Once upon a time, say the Ackawoi, there was on the savannah above the fall an Indian settlement in which lived an old man so worn out and useless from age that in his feet the jiggers buried themselves unmolested. In short, the old man was a scandal and a nuisance to his fellows. So the latter put the old man with his pegall into a woodskin, which they then launched on the river and allowed to drift over the fall.

title.en: Fabled Peoples: the Night-Folk of Canakoo and the Hooronis
title.zh: 幻族：卡納庫夜民與呼魯尼人

region.zh: 蓋亞那卡納庫山與帕卡賴馬

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: Traveling round the Canakoo mountains, im Thurn was often told of a certain tribe who lived up among the highest rocks and never came down into the plain except by night; fires may sometimes be seen up in these mountains by night. The Hooronis are a tribe living beyond the Pacaraimas, men by night but fish by day: if an Indian of another tribe finds his way into a Hooroni house and tries to put one of the apparent fish over the fire to roast, all the fish change back into men and slay the intruder. Another tribe lives like ordinary Indians by day but retires into the water at night, sleeping standing with only their heads above water. On Roraima the Indians say there are huge white jaguars and huge white eagles; and the di-dis, beings in shape something between men and monkeys, live in the forests near the river banks — the being that suggested to Charles Waterton his famous nondescript.
summary.zh: 卡納庫山中有一族，居最高之巖，惟夜始下平原；夜間山上有火光。呼魯尼人者，居帕卡賴馬之外，晝為魚夜為人：他族人入其屋，見魚而烹之，則魚皆復為人而殺之。又有一族，晝如常人，夜入水而立眠，僅露其首。羅賴馬山有白虎白鷹之屬；迪迪者，形介人猴之間，居河畔之林——華特頓氏怪物標本，蓋本於此。

sensitivity.note: Guiana oral tradition recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: When travelling round the Canakoo mountains, im Thurn was often told by the Indians of a certain tribe of Indians who lived up among the highest rocks and who never came down into the plain except by night. Indians who have ventured up into the mountains have often heard sounds from the settlements of these people; and even from below one may often see their fires by night — an appearance as of fire to be seen sometimes up in these mountains.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Other people of the same kind are the Hooronis, a tribe of Indians living beyond the Pacaraimas, who are men by night but fish by day: even by day they do not live in the water, but lie about their houses as do fish caught for food by ordinary Indians. But if by chance an Indian of another tribe finds his way into the house of a Hooroni, and, thinking it empty, helps himself to any of the apparent fish lying about, and tries to put this fish over the fire to roast, then all the fish change back into men and slay the intruder. Another favourite statement of the Indians is that there is another tribe who live like ordinary Indians by day, but retire into the water at night and sleep standing, with only their heads above water.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: Again, any extraordinary or inaccessible rock is always said to be inhabited by monstrous animals: on Roraima the Indians say that there are huge white jaguars and huge white eagles. To this class probably belongs the di-dis, beings in shape something between men and monkeys, who live in the forests near the river banks — a being which has some literary interest as probably that which suggested to Charles Waterton the idea of constructing his famous nondescript.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Haiarri Root: Grown from a Son's Blood

region.zh: 蓋亞那阿拉瓦克之地（據布雷特）

texts.period: Arawak tradition recorded by Brett; retold 1883 (im Thurn)

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: Once upon a time an Indian took his young son to bathe. Wherever the lad swam the fish died; and the father found by experiment that these fish were quite wholesome as food, so he made a practice of obtaining fish in this way. But after a time the fish, having taken counsel, chose a moment when the lad sat on a log just before plunging into the water — when, therefore, the fish could approach him safely — and then, all springing out of the water together, struck their spines into the lad. The wound made in this way by the sting-ray proved fatal. But as the father was carrying his dying son home, the blood dropped on to the ground, and wherever it fell there grew up a haiarri plant, which has ever since been used by Indians to poison the streams when they want to catch fish.
summary.zh: 昔一印第安人攜幼子浴於河；童所游處，魚皆斃，而其肉可食。父遂習以為常。魚會議定計：俟童坐木未下水之際，群躍出水，以刺螫之。魟之傷致命。父負垂死之子歸；血滴於地，滴處皆生海阿黎——印第安人至今以之毒水取魚。

sensitivity.note: Arawak tradition from Brett, retold by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

title.en: The Arawaks against Meyanow and the Caribs
title.zh: 阿拉瓦克戰梅亞瑙與加勒比

region.zh: 蓋亞那波默龍河阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: Everard F. im Thurn, Among the Indians of Guiana (1883), ch. XVIII 'Folk-lore'

summary.en: The Arawaks say that their ancestors had first to fight a fierce tribe called Meyanow; and after they had exterminated these they were harassed by the Caribs, who came first from the islands and then settled on the mainland. Every year the Caribs from all quarters gathered round the Arawaks on the Pomeroon and attacked them. One year the Arawaks chose a chief, placed their men in ambush on each side of the path from the river to the settlement, and when the Caribs fell into it, exhausted their arrows on them and finished with war-clubs till the few survivors, their retreat cut off, were all slain. The next year the chief hid the women and children, laid a huge tree-trunk under water across the mouth of a side stream, and sent a light canoe to lure the enemy: the pursuing Caribs' heavy canoes struck the unsuspected barrier and were split, and the Arawaks rushed out and slew almost all. A third time the Caribs came, and were again overthrown; their chief, struck in the face by a three-pronged fish arrow, was captured alive — and the Arawaks determined to let him go unharmed; and this was the end of the feud between the tribes.
summary.zh: 阿拉瓦克人言其先戰梅亞瑙族而滅之；繼為加勒比所擾。歲歲加勒比合圍波默龍。一歲，阿拉瓦克擇酋設伏於河路兩側；敵入伏，箭盡而以戰棒斃之，無一得脫。次歲，匿婦孺，沈巨木於支流之口，以輕舟誘敵；敵舟疾追，觸暗木而裂；眾出而幾盡殲之。三歲又至，又敗；其酋面中三叉魚箭而被擒。阿拉瓦克縱之無傷——二族之仇，至此而終。

sensitivity.note: Arawak historical legend recorded by im Thurn 1883; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: The Arawaks say that their ancestors had first to fight a fierce tribe called Meyanow; and after they had exterminated these they were harassed by the Caribs, who came first from the islands, but afterwards settled on the mainland and carried on an even more constant warfare. Every year the Caribs from all quarters gathered round the Arawaks on the Pomeroon and attacked them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: One year, when the Caribs were expected, the Arawaks chose a chief to lead them against the enemy. Having seen that large quantities of arrows had been provided, he placed his men in ambush, some distance from the river, at each side of the path leading from the river to the settlement. When the Caribs came they fell into the ambush: the Arawaks exhausted their arrows, fell upon the enemy with their war-clubs, and not a Carib of that whole party escaped.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next year the chief made all his men hide their women and children in safety in the forest, placed the huge trunk of a tree across the mouth of a side stream just under water, and sent a small boat of very light draught to lure the enemy: the pursuing Caribs' large and heavy canoes struck heavily against the unsuspected barrier and were split, and the Arawaks rushed out from their hiding-places and slew almost all. Yet a third time the Caribs came, and were again overthrown; their chief, struck in the face by a three-pronged fish arrow, was captured alive — and the Arawaks determined to let him go unharmed; and this was the end of the feud between the tribes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of im Thurn 1883, ch. XVIII; not verbatim.
